title: The Epistemic Rise of Accounting Research in Financial Economics: A Historical Study on the Conception of the Usefulness of Accounting
publisher_note: A full English translation of this article follows the version in French.
abstract: The study published by Ball and Brown in 1968 is mainly recognized for its assertion that the accounting of the time was useful to investors, which contradicted the normative accounting literature then considered the authority. This idea was not self-evident, and we aim in this paper to better understand how the assertion initially introduced in Ball and Brown's article became firmly established in an important stream of academic accounting literature: “empirical” accounting research in financial economics. We conduct a historical study, drawing on some concepts from the “sociology of translation,” to examine the rise of accounting research in financial economics, which unfolded through several reinterpretations of the concept of utility—shifting from stock market valuation to the framing of contractual clauses, in addition to the discovery of market anomalies. Our analyses highlight, on the one hand, the social processes surrounding the emergence and development of accounting research in financial economics and, on the other hand, the fragility and vagueness of the foundations upon which this type of research was built. Contradicting the claim that accounting research in financial economics naturally prevailed due to its superiority in terms of knowledge, we argue that the fragility and vagueness of that perspective, instead of undermining its credibility, contributed to establishing a climate of conceptual ambiguity that was conducive to its propagation. This ambiguity is expressed at two levels: ambiguous mobilization of the efficient market hypothesis, and semantic ambiguity in the conception of the usefulness of accounting information. More generally, our article adds to the discussion of “travels of ideas” and “boundary gatekeeping” surrounding established ideas.
